tips.section: Danish Red and White Chevron Signs
tips.text: Danish chevrons are white with a red arrow. Very important: Similar chevrons can be found in many European countries. Here, we are focusing on the key differences between Northern European countries - among them, Denmark is the only one with red-and-white chevrons. Note: Very rarely, similar chevrons can also be found in the Faroe Islands.

tips.section: Swedish Yellow and Blue Chevron Signs
tips.text: Swedish chevrons and hazard markers feature a yellow-and-blue color scheme that is unique in Europe. This distinctive combination is an excellent clue for identifying Sweden.
In Norway, Finland, and Iceland, chevron signs feature a black background with a yellow arrow. Note: Similar chevrons can also be found in other European countries, such as Portugal or Ireland.
Denmark can have rounded metal signposts that extend around the entire sign. This feature is unique to Denmark.

Finland, Iceland, and Sweden use road signs with a red border and yellow center, making them a useful regional clue. Important: In Finland, signs often feature a thin yellow border around the red area. This design is not found in other countries. Note: Norway uses similar signs with a white center instead.

Unlike Iceland, Finland and Sweden, Norway uses red-white signs. Notes: - Norwegian road signs often feature four bolts arranged in a rectangular pattern. - This feature is not unique to Norway in Northern Europe, but it can help distinguish Norway from its neighboring countries, Finland and Sweden, especially in difficult rounds.
Among Northern European countries, Sweden and Finland are the only ones where you can find road signs with a blue-and-white post. Note: Similar signposts can also be found in Estonia and Luxembourg.
In Sweden, you can often find distinctive road signposts painted red and yellow. This is a unique feature of Sweden and can be a useful clue when identifying the country.

Wooden snow poles with reflectors are a unique feature of Norway’s road infrastructure. Note: Wooden snow poles can also be found in other northern countries, but they almost never have reflectors attached to them.
Swedish snow poles are usually red-orange, with a tall white reflector positioned slightly above the middle of the pole. Important: Some poles have a second, thinner reflector above the main one.

Norwegian snow poles are usually red-orange and feature a fairly narrow white reflector. The reflector is generally positioned closer to the middle of the pole. Note: Swedish snow poles usually have a wider reflector, positioned slightly higher, while Finnish snow poles have the reflector at the very top of the pole.

In Finland, you can often find red-orange snow poles with a thin white stripe near the top. Note: In Norway and Sweden, snow poles often have a wider white stripe positioned lower down. They can also feature multiple white stripes, while Finnish snow poles usually have only one stripe.
In Norway, you can occasionally encounter a rarer type of snow pole painted black. Black snow poles are found almost exclusively in Norway. Note: These poles may have one or two reflectors.
The Danish pedestrian crossing sign features five zebra stripes touching the blue background. The pedestrian also appears somewhat “shy,” with a distinctive posture that helps set the sign apart.

Norwegian pedestrian crossing signs usually feature four zebra stripes and come in two main silhouette variants: - a simple, stylized figure - a more detailed figure wearing a hat. Note: There is also a variant with five stripes, but it is much less common.

Icelandic pedestrian crossing signs feature four stripes and often have a slightly yellowish tint. Note: Iceland is the only European country where pedestrian crossing signs with a yellow background are used.
Swedish pedestrian crossing signs feature four zebra stripes. Interestingly, Sweden also has a variant featuring a female silhouette, known as Fru Gårman.
Pedestrian crossing signs in Finland feature five stripes and generally come in two variants: - with a more detailed pedestrian figure - with a simplified, more schematic figure
On the Faroe Islands, especially in the largest city, Tórshavn, pedestrian crossings are often additionally marked with a vertical blue-and-white striped panel attached to the signpost.
Directional signs in Denmark have a very distinctive appearance. They are often placed very close to the ground and typically come in red-and-white or blue-and-white color combinations.

In Sweden, alongside the more common blue directional signs, you can also find yellow signs with black text and a red border. This color combination is unique among directional signs in Northern Europe. Note: The places marked by these yellow signs are generally very small settlements, which can make them surprisingly difficult to find on the map.

In Sweden, most directional signs feature a blue background with white text and a white border. The direction is indicated by a thin arrow. Note: Finland also uses blue directional signs, but the white arrows are noticeably thicker than those used on Swedish signs.

Finnish directional signs feature a solid blue background, white text, and a white border, with arrows indicating the direction of travel. Key feature: The directional arrows are made up of solid white triangles pointing in the direction of travel.

Norwegian road signs have a distinctive yellow background with a black border. Road numbers are usually displayed either in a green box for European routes and major roads, or in a white box for secondary roads. Note: Similar or very similar directional signs can also be found in the Faroe Islands and Iceland, in addition to Norway.
In Denmark, outer road lines will often be white squares or small rectangles.

On rural roads in Sweden, the outer road lines are made up of short white dashed markings. This is a useful clue that can help you identify Swedish roads with confidence. Note: Similar markings can occur in other European countries, such as Estonia, but they are particularly common in Sweden.

On smaller roads in Norway, long dashed white edge lines are commonly used. This is different from Sweden, where dashed edge lines are noticeably shorter. Note: On larger roads in Norway, the edge lines are solid, while the center lines are yellow.
On Swedish highways, the outer road lines can feature a distinctive pattern of small white rectangles arranged diagonally in groups of three or four per row.

Road markings in Denmark are white, and double center lines are very common. This is a useful clue when identifying Danish roads. Note: Similar road markings can also be found elsewhere in Europe, particularly in Poland and Greece.
In Norway, road markings are often made up of small dots of paint, creating a distinctive dotted appearance.

On some major roads in Norway, the center lines are yellow and, importantly, often have a distinct orange tint. Note: In Northern Europe, Finland is generally the only other country where yellow center lines can be found. However, yellow road markings are gradually being phased out there, and the existing markings typically do not have the same noticeable orange tint as those in Norway.
Guardrail posts in Norway are often made of wood, which is relatively uncommon in other Northern European countries.

Guardrails on the Faroe Islands are often equipped with yellow reflectors. Note: Yellow reflectors are not used on guardrails in the other Nordic countries, making this a particularly useful distinction within Northern Europe.
In Denmark, you can find square or B-Profile guardrails without reflectors. Note: Denmark is the only country in Northern Europe where this type of guardrail is commonly found.

The standard Swedish bollard has a wedge-shaped form. It features a rectangular white reflector at the front and two white dots at the back. The black band is slightly slanted. Notes: - The reflectors can also be orange or yellow - Similar bollards can be found in many European countries, for example, in Lithuania.

The most typical bollards in Finland have a cylindrical shape, with the black section containing the reflector wrapping continuously around the entire post and featuring a slanted shape. Key feature: the black section forms a continuous band around the whole bollard and featuring a slanted shape. Note: In Finland, a similar hollow, curved bollard can also be found.
Iceland uses a distinctive yellow plastic bollard with a diagonally cut top. It features a large grey reflector on the front.
Faroese roadside posts are small wooden poles, usually painted yellow or yellow and red.

Denmark has unique and easily recognisable bollards. These are white, wedge-shaped bollards with a large rectangular panel featuring yellow-and-white diagonal markings. Above it is an orange reflective strip. Sometimes, a removable black number plate can be found below the reflector.

In Norway, the most common bollards are thin, curved, rectangular posts with a reflector positioned inside a black parallelogram. Key feature: the bollard is flat, and the reflector is set inside the black parallelogram.
The second type of bollard found in Sweden is cylindrical, with a straight black band that wraps continuously around the entire bollard.
The third type of bollard found in Sweden is flat, with a black band that does not wrap around the entire post. Key Feature: The reflector is usually rectangular.

The Swedish road sign with a white M on a blue background is used on narrow roads where two vehicles cannot easily pass each other. Key detail: the middle part of the M does not extend to the bottom of the letter. Note: A similar sign can also be found in Norway, but the design is different. On the Norwegian version, the middle part of the M extends all the way to the bottom.

The Norwegian road sign with a white letter M on a blue background is used on narrow roads where two vehicles have difficulty passing each other. Key feature: the middle part of the M extends all the way to the bottom. Note: A similar sign is used in Sweden, but there the middle part of the M does not extend to the bottom.
A small cap on top of wooden utility poles is a common feature in Norway, Sweden, and Finland. Note: This feature is also commonly found in Estonia and Latvia.
This distinctive sign with a metal tube frame marks the entrance to a city. On the way out, it is crossed out with a red diagonal line.
In residential areas of Norway, white signs marked “Sone” are commonly used to indicate speed limits. Note: It is also worth noting that Norwegian road signs often have four bolts.

These wooden markers used to identify power lines often feature a blue-and-white stripe or a solid blue stripe at the top. They can frequently be found near electricity poles and power-line structures.
The country-code top-level domain .no is assigned to Norway.
The country-code top-level domain .se is assigned to Sweden.
The country-code top-level domain .is is assigned to Iceland.
The country-code top-level domain .fi is assigned to Finland.
The country-code top-level domain .dk is assigned to Denmark.
The country-code top-level domain .fo is assigned to the Faroe Islands.
Most Danish street names end in "vej", the Danish word for "road" or "way". Street signs are most commonly blue with white lettering.

Swedish street names commonly use the suffixes "vägen" and "gatan". On street signs, these are often abbreviated to "v" and "g", respectively. The words "väg" and "gata" can also appear as standalone words.
The most common suffixes in Norwegian street names are "vei" and "gate". When attached to a street name, they can appear as "-veien", "-gata", or "-gate".
Most Finnish street names end in "-tie" or "-katu", while "-polku" and "-kuja" are also common. Street signs typically have a white background with black text
The letter Ðð is used in only two places: Iceland and the Faroe Islands. Seeing this distinctive letter in text can therefore be a strong clue that you are looking at Icelandic or Faroese.
The letter Þþ is used in the Icelandic alphabet and is a distinctive feature of the Icelandic language. It is not used in Faroese, making it a particularly useful clue for identifying Icelandic text.

In Northern Europe, the letter Ö can be found in Finland, Sweden, and Iceland. It is a useful clue when identifying text from these countries. Note: Beyond these countries, Ö is also used in Turkish, Hungarian, German, and Estonian.
Among the Nordic countries, the letter Ä is used in Finland and Sweden, making it a useful clue when identifying text from these countries. Note: The letter Ä is also used in Estonian and German.
The letter Ø is used in the Norwegian, Danish, and Faroese alphabets. It is a distinctive Scandinavian letter and can be a useful clue when identifying these languages.
Among the Northern European countries, the letter Å is used in Norway, Denmark, Sweden, and Finland. Note: In Finland, Å is used in Swedish-language names and is considered a Swedish letter.
The letter Æ is used in Denmark, Norway, Iceland, and the Faroe Islands. It can be a useful clue when identifying text from these countries and regions.
In Denmark and Sweden, some commercial license plate is a fully yellow plate with the blue stripe on the left side Identical (non-commercial) in: Netherlands Luxembourg UK (rear ones only)
The Norwegian commercial license plate is very distinctive, as it is mainly turquoise green. It also features a blue strip on the left, similar to the blue bands found on European license plates.

tips.section: White Gen 3 Car with a Long Antenna
tips.text: In Sweden, Finland, and Iceland, you can find a white Gen 3 car with a long antenna. Note: This car can also be found in Norway and Denmark, but it is extremely rare in both countries.

In Iceland Gen 4 coverage features two pickup trucks - one white and one red. They are usually completely blurred, although their color can sometimes be slightly visible. Important: The pickup can be identified by the shape of the blur. Around the cabin area, the blur slightly widens on both sides, following the shape of the vehicle. Note: A pickup can also be found in the Faroe Islands, but it has an antenna at the front, which helps distinguish it from the Icelandic pickup.

On the Faroe Islands, Gen 4 coverage was captured using a black pickup truck with an antenna at the front. The truck is always blurred in the imagery. Note: The pickup used in Iceland does not have this type of antenna.
Among the Northern European countries, Sweden is the only one where a RED car Gen 4 can be found. The car can appear with or without an antenna.
Among the Northern European countries, Sweden is the only one where a white Gen 4 car can be found. The car can appear with or without an antenna.

tips.section: Blue Car Gen 4 in Northern Europe
tips.text: A blue car Gen 4 can be found in Denmark, Norway, Finland, and Sweden. The antenna may sometimes be vidible.

K-Market and S-Market are two major Finnish supermarket chains, both featuring distinctive and easily recognizable logos. These supermarket brands are exclusive to Finland. Note: K-Market can sometimes be confused with other K-group supermarket brands, such as K-Supermarket and K-Citymarket.

The pig bank on the Bónus supermarket logo in Iceland looks cute, but it is not as “goofy” as the one found in the Faroe Islands. In 2021, Bónus underwent a rebranding, and the pig lost its distinctive crooked eye. This can be a useful way to distinguish Iceland from the Faroe Islands. Exception: The Bónus store in Vestmannaeyjabær on the island of Heimaey may still feature the old Faroese-style pig. Thanks to @irrational_14195 for this meta!

tips.section: Bónus Pig on the Faroe Islands
tips.text: On the Faroe Islands, you can find Bónus supermarkets, recognizable by their logo featuring a pink piggy bank with an incredibly comical and slightly “goofy” facial expression and its distinctive crooked eye. Key feature: the pig’s crooked eye. Thanks to @irrational_14195 for this meta!
